extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and construing means- (or step-) plus-function claim limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (and pre-AIA 112 sixth paragraph), including making prima facie equivalence rejections, evaluating applicant proof of nonequivalence, related 112 rejections, and form paragraphs for Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case of equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner finds that a prior art element (A) performs the function specified in the claim, (B) is not excluded by any explicit definition provided in the specification for an equivalent, and (C) is an equivalent of the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation, the examiner should provide an explanation and rationale in the Office action as to why the prior art element is an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explanation and rationale in the Office action (see In re Bond). If the examiner shows at least one of the supporting factors for equivalence (see MPEP § 2183), conclude the claimed limitation is met by the prior art element. The examiner should also demonstrate, where appropriate, why it would have been obvious to substitute applicant’s described structure, material, or acts for that described in the prior art reference (see In re Brown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors supporting a conclusion that the prior art element is an equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: Three indicia that will support concluding a prior art element is an equivalent to the corresponding element disclosed in the specification: (A) performs the identical function in substantially the same way and produces substantially the same results; (B) a person of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized the interchangeability of the element shown in the prior art for the corresponding element disclosed in the specification; (C) there are insubstantial differences between the prior art element and the corresponding element disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite relevant case law examples (e.g., Kemco Sales, Deere & Co., IMS Technology, Warner-Jenkinson). Consider 'function, way, and result' (Graver Tank concepts). If one of these indicia is shown, it should be sufficient to support equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate obviousness of substitution when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to concluding that a prior art element is an equivalent, the examiner should demonstrate, where appropriate, why it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time to substitute the applicant’s described structure, material, or acts for that described in the prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use In re Brown and related precedent. If obviousness is established it may support a 102/103 rejection even when equivalence/nonequivalence issues exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shifts to applicant to show nonequivalence after prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the examiner establishes a prima facie case of equivalence, the burden shifts to the applicant to show that the element shown in the prior art is not an equivalent of the structure, material or acts disclosed in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No further analysis of equivalents is required of the examiner until applicant disagrees and provides reasons and/or evidence (see In re Mulder, In re Walter, In re Swinehart). If applicant provides persuasive reasons/evidence, examine those in light of MPEP § 2184 guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even if nonequivalence shown, examiner must consider obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant shows that the prior art element is not an equivalent, the examiner must still make a 35 U.S.C. 103 analysis to determine if the claimed means- (or step-) plus-function would have been obvious from the prior art to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of nonequivalence prevents anticipation but does not prevent a determination of obviousness. Apply 102/103 rejections where appropriate (including when balance of claim limitations are anticipated by the prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant may bear burden when specification is silent about equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification is silent as to what constitutes equivalents and the examiner has made out a prima facie case of equivalence, the burden is placed upon the applicant to show that a prior art element which performs the claimed function is not an equivalent of the structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant reasons may include: (A) teachings in the applicant’s specification that particular prior art is not equivalent; (B) teachings in the prior art reference that tend to show nonequivalence; (C) 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit evidence of facts tending to show nonequivalence (see In re Noll, Hybritech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of limitations must be consistent with the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: When the applicant relies on teachings in the applicant’s own specification, the examiner must ensure the applicant is interpreting the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation consistent with the disclosure in the specification; if the specification defines what is meant by the limitation for the purposes of the claimed invention, the examiner should interpret the limitation as having that meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no definition is provided use judgment to determine scope. The scope of equivalents depends on how the element is described; a claim may be limited to particular structure/material/acts or may embrace equivalents, depending on the disclosure (see NOMOS, Ishida). Avoid reading limitations broader or narrower than the specification supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence requires performance of the identical function
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless an element performs the identical function specified in the claim, it cannot be an equivalent for the purposes of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 112 sixth paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Pennwalt and related authority. First establish identity of function, then examine 'way' and 'result' indicia; there is no single litmus test for equivalence—use multiple indicia from MPEP § 2183.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere allegations of nonequivalence are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A bare statement or opinion by applicant that the element shown in the prior art is not an equivalent is not persuasive; the examiner should consider and weigh indicia and evidence presented and determine whether, on balance, the applicant has met the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant argues limitation is limited to specific characteristics not described in the specification, the claim should not be allowed until amended to recite those specific structural or additional functional characteristics. Examiner should require factual or documentary support (see MPEP § 2184, In re Fitzgerald, Swinehart).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant may amend claims to avoid equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may amend claims during prosecution to (1) further limit the function so there is no longer identity of function with the prior art element, or (2) replace the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation with specific structure, material or acts that are not described in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise applicant of these options when appropriate; amendments may resolve 112(f) or prior art issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider related rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/(b) when corresponding structure lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: If a means- (or step-) plus-function limitation is not supported by corresponding structure, material or acts in the specification disclosure, the examiner should consider rejections under: (A) 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for lack of enablement; (B) 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for lack of adequate written description; (C) 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (A) apparatus block diagrams without structure may still be enabling if structure is conventional and determinable without undue experimentation (In re Ghiron); (B) computer-implemented means/algorithm lacking sufficient disclosure may require a written description rejection (see MPEP § 2161.01, § 2181 IV); (C) cite Noah Systems, In re Aoyama, Finisar for indefiniteness concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship to the doctrine of equivalents (DOE)
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE arises in infringement litigation; in determining equivalence under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) during examination, decisions involving the DOE should be considered but should not unduly influence the 112(f) determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essential inquiry is whether a substitute matches the function, way, and result of the claimed element (Warner-Jenkinson). But 112(f) applies a restrictive role—limit broad functional language to corresponding structure described in the specification and equivalents thereof; treat DOE precedent as informative but not controlling for ex parte examination (see MPEP § 2186).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-prong test for invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and rebuttable presumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation meets the three-prong test and will be interpreted under 112(f) when: (A) the limitation uses the term 'means' or 'step' or a generic placeholder substitute; (B) the placeholder is modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or similar); and (C) the placeholder is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this test in form paragraph 7.30.05. The use of 'means' creates a rebuttable presumption that 112(f) applies; absence of 'means' creates a rebuttable presumption that 112(f) does not apply. The presumptions are rebutted when claim language establishes sufficient structure/material/acts or conversely recites only function without sufficient structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoking 112(f) despite absence of the word 'means' (form ¶7.30.06)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that do not use 'means' may nonetheless be interpreted under 112(f) when they use a generic placeholder coupled with functional language without reciting sufficient structure to perform the recited function and the generic placeholder is not preceded by a structural modifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify such claim limitations and inform applicant. If applicant does not intend such an interpretation, they may amend the limitation to recite sufficient structure or show that sufficient structure is present. Use form paragraph 7.30.06 once in an Office action where applicable and identify the claim/limitations involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invoking 112(f) despite presence of 'means' (form ¶7.30.07)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that uses 'means' or 'step' may nonetheless not be interpreted under 112(f) when the limitation recites sufficient structure, materials, or acts to entirely perform the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify such limitations and inform applicant. If applicant intends 112(f) treatment, they may amend to remove the structure/materials/acts or show lack of sufficient structure. Use form paragraph 7.30.07 once in an Office action where applicable and identify the claim/limitations involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies when disclosure of corresponding structure is lacking or not clearly linked (form ¶7.34.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: When disclosure of the structure, material, or acts for performing the function recited in a claim is lacking, insufficient, or not clearly linked, the examiner should suggest remedies such as: (a) amending the written description to expressly recite corresponding structure/material/acts and clearly link them to the claimed function without new matter; or (b) stating on the record what corresponding structure/material/acts, implicitly or inherently set forth in the specification, perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Office action, specify the limitation invoking 112(f) and explain why disclosure is insufficient (e.g., no structure that performs the function, structure does not perform the entire function, or no association between structure and function). Refer applicant to 37 CFR 1.75(d), MPEP §§ 608.01(o), 2181 for additional guidance.
